title: Metrics and alerting
summary: Time-series ingestion, compression, downsampling and alerts.
prompt: Design a metrics platform: thousands of services emit counters, gauges and histograms; engineers build dashboards and alert rules; alerts must fire reliably even when parts of the platform are struggling.

requirements: Functional: ingest labelled time series, query by metric and label filters with aggregation over time ranges, evaluate alert rules, notify on-call.
Non-functional: ingest without loss at peak, recent queries in ~1 s, retain raw data for 2 weeks and downsampled data for a year, alerting more available than dashboards.
estimation: 20M active series sampled every 10 s ⇒ 2M samples/s.
With delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR-compressed values, samples average roughly 1–2 bytes: ~170–350 GB a day raw.
Cardinality is the real risk: one label with user IDs can create millions of new series.
api: Ingest: agents push batches {series labels, timestamp, value} (or the platform scrapes endpoints).
Query: a range query like sum by (service)(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) over a time range and step.
Alert rules: {expression, for: duration, severity, routing}.
data: Series identified by metric name + sorted labels, hashed to a series ID; an inverted index maps label=value to series IDs.
Samples stored in compressed blocks per series covering fixed time windows (e.g. 2 h), then compacted into larger blocks.
Downsampled rollups (5 min, 1 h) with min, max, sum and count, so averages stay correct.
design: Agents → ingestion gateways → a durable log partitioned by series hash → storage nodes that build in-memory head blocks and flush to object storage.
Query service fans out to storage nodes (recent data) and to object storage (older blocks), then merges.
The alert evaluator runs rules on a schedule against recent data and sends firing alerts to a notifier that deduplicates, groups and routes them.
deepDives: Cardinality control: per-tenant limits on active series, reject or drop new label values beyond the limit, and report the worst offenders.
Histograms: store bucket counts so percentiles can be aggregated across instances; averaging per-instance p99s is wrong.
Alerting reliability: run evaluators redundantly in pairs with deduplication, keep them close to fresh data, and alert when metrics go missing (the absence of data is a signal).
bottlenecks: Expensive queries over long ranges and many series: query limits, caching of results per step, and automatic use of rollups.
Ingestion spikes from deploys or restarts: the log buffers bursts; storage catches up.
Meta-monitoring: monitor the monitoring system from an independent, simpler stack.
tradeoffs: Push vs pull: pull simplifies health detection and rate control; push suits short-lived jobs and serverless functions.
Long retention at full resolution is expensive; rollups lose detail for old data.
Strict cardinality limits protect the platform but can drop data teams expected to keep.

rubric.text: Sized samples per second and storage with compression.
Modelled series with labels and an inverted index.
Buffered ingestion with a durable log.
Used downsampled rollups for long retention.
Designed alert evaluation, deduplication and routing.
Controlled cardinality with limits and visibility.
Made alerting more reliable than dashboards, including meta-monitoring.
